summary_findings: Four communities carry a star nomenclature deep enough to be called a system, and they are not the ones a Sanskrit database would predict. The Mundas are first by a distance: Hoffmann's Encyclopaedia Mundarica vol. VII (cols. 1919-1925, s.v. ipil) is a seven-page star map with about thirty named objects, a plate, and a stated method, and it opens by saying that the Munda 'neither knows, nor cares to know, what a horoscope is'. Santali is second, through Campbell (1899) and Bodding vol. V (1936); Kurukh has eight or nine names in Grignard (1924); Gondi has a large modern field survey (Vahia & Halkare 2013, in copyright, paraphrased here) and essentially nothing in the colonial record. Toda has Rivers (1906) — three pages, but unusually careful, and he drew the Great Bear on paper to have it named rather than trusting a verbal description. Ho, Khasi, Nicobarese and Andamanese yield a handful of terms each. The organising principles are agricultural and domestic rather than zodiacal: nothing here divides the ecliptic, nothing tracks the moon's monthly stations, and where the nakshatra system does surface it has been converted into something else — Santali ruhni is not Aldebaran but the seven-day sowing week in Jeṭ, and Bodding marks the planet names sukro and Sani '(only in books)', meaning they are printed but not spoken. Three figures recur across unrelated language families and are the real find. (1) Ursa Major is a cot: Santali buḍhi parkom ipil 'the old woman's cot', Kurukh khaṭī-pāwā bīnkō 'the cot-feet constellation' with the three handle stars called ḍhālbar 'thieves', Gondi Sedona Katul with Kalher 'thieves' and a story that the old woman must never fall asleep or the world ends, and — printed in 1916, before any of the fieldwork — the Chhattisgarhi Dhuri belief that the Great Bear is a cot with three thieves tied to it. Mundari alone turns the same cot into a bier, with Alioth and Mizar as mourners walking away from the grave. (2) Orion is a plough or a yoke, never a hunter: Santali and Mundari araṛ ipilko 'the yoke stars', Mundari siṭan ipil 'the ploughman' for Rigel, Kurukh ugtā-pagṛī bīnkō, Gondi Nangar. Only the Toda break this, reading the sword as a porcupine the belt stars are running away from. (3) The Milky Way is a road with livestock on it: Mundari gaiko hora 'the cattle road', walked by Lugu, Siṅgboṅga's cowherd, who is himself the morning star; Kurukh gāy-chour bīnkō, the cattle-track out of the village; Gondi Dhor Sari, the path of the animals; Santali hat dahar, the market road. Only the seafaring Nicobarese make it water — dāk-oal-kalahoiya, 'river in the sky'. A fourth, subtler thread is a bird on a nest with something thrown at it: Mundari putam ipil (the dove, Aldebaran) with jarom ipilkiŋ (her two eggs) and muṅgaru ipilko (the mallet flung at her, the Pleiades); Santali potam bele (the pigeon's eggs, ε Lyrae) with bele kombro (the egg thief, Vega); Gondi Purad and Mes (a bird and its eggs) with the Pleiades thrown at them. Three recorders working a century apart, three different parts of the sky, one story. Meteors are the excrement of the stars in Santali (ipil ic'), Mundari (ipilko ic') and Gondi (sukum pelkta) alike, which follows from stars being living beings — in Ho they are grammatically animate, as Burrows' paradigm ipil / ipilkiŋ / ipilko shows, while trees are not. Comets are a broom in Mundari, Kurukh and Gondi, and in Khasi a star smoking a pipe ('lur-dih-duma). DRY SOURCES, recorded as findings rather than omitted. Bhili: nothing. Neither Russell & Hiralal's Bhil article nor any public-domain dictionary gives a Bhil star name; the only substantial treatment is Shetye, Halkare & Sule, JAHH 26(2), 441-468 (2023), which is in copyright and which could not be obtained in full, so no Bhili entry is offered rather than a guessed one. Naga: Hodson's The Naga Tribes of Manipur (1911) has sun- and moon-worship at Mao, an eclipse rite and a dog-and-moon tale, and not one star name; searched for Pleiades, Orion, Great Bear, Milky Way, pole star and constellation with zero hits. Khasi: Gurdon's The Khasis (1907) likewise yields only Ka Sngi (the sun, feminine) and U Bynai (the moon, masculine) and the story of the moon's spots — every Khasi entry here comes from Nissor Singh's dictionary instead, and the English-Khasi dictionary of 1920 was rejected because its 'Milky Way' is a translator's descriptive coinage, not a Khasi name. Andamanese: Man found exactly one named constellation in the whole archipelago (bela-, Orion's Belt), and Radcliffe-Brown forty years later in the North Andaman states flatly that individual stars and constellations are not recognised there at all — the stars are simply Catlo, the big ones, named for a beetle, and Katan, the small ones, named for the firefly. Russell & Hiralal's four volumes, grepped end to end, produced sky cosmology (Bhuiya, Turi, Dumal) but only one community with named figures, the Dhuri. DSAL hosts no Munda, Kurukh, Gondi, Bhili, Khasi or Andamanese dictionary at all. Bodding's Santal Dictionary is on the Internet Archive only as vol. V, so his entries for arar ipil, buḍhi parkom and ipil itself could not be read; likewise Encyclopaedia Mundarica vols. IX, XI and XIV-XVI are missing, which is why several Mundari names rest on the ipil article alone.

entries.region: Santal Parganas, Jharkhand / adjoining Bengal and Odisha
entries.literal_meaning: the Soren people (a Santal sept name in the animate plural)
entries.usage_note: The totem of the Soren sept; the position of the cluster before dawn is used to tell the time of night. Campbell's illustrative sentence asks in which quarter of the sky the Pleiades stand at dawn.
entries.citation: Campbell, A Santali-English Dictionary (1899), s.v. Sorenko, p. 594
entries.quote: Sorenko. The Pleiades, or seven stars in Taurus. The Pleiad is the totem of the Soren sept of Santals. Netar Sorenko do okare aligaakokana? Just now where (in what part of the heavens) are the Pleiades at dawn?
entries.notes: One of the twelve Santal septs is Soren; the cluster and the sept share the name, so the Pleiades are a clan totem rather than a calendrical mansion. Nothing in Campbell's entry derives from the nakshatra system.

entries.region: Santal Parganas, Jharkhand / adjoining Bengal and Odisha
entries.usage_note: Used to tell the hour of the night: 'the Pleiades have reached half down the western sky' marks roughly the position the sun holds at 3 p.m. Bodding also records the figure that joins the Pleiades to Orion: the cluster is the mallet belonging to the arar lalak.
entries.citation: Bodding, A Santal Dictionary, vol. V (1936), s.v. sɘren (ipil), p. 352
entries.quote: s.ko do arar lalakko reak murgar kantakoa, the Pleiades are the mallet of the arar lalakko (three small stars near the belt of Orion)
entries.notes: Bodding's headword is printed with a hooked vowel that the DjVu OCR renders as 'sgren'; the reading sɘren follows Campbell's Sorenko and the sept name Soren. The mallet-and-yoke figure is the one Hoffmann records at length for Mundari (muṅgaru ipilko), which is strong mutual confirmation across two independent lexicographers.

entries.region: Santal Parganas, Jharkhand / adjoining Bengal and Odisha
entries.usage_note: Its rising is announced as an event: 'the Yoke constellation has risen'. The same word is the ordinary word for a yoke of oxen (miṭ arar sadom).
entries.citation: Campbell, A Santali-English Dictionary (1899), s.v. Arar, p. 19
entries.quote: Arar. The Yoke constellation, being the three stars in Orion's belt. Arar ipilko rakaḥtakana. The Yoke constellation has risen.
entries.notes: Sanskrit names no asterism for the belt alone — Mṛgaśīrṣa and Invakāḥ are the stars of Orion's head — so there is no Sanskrit counterpart to link. The identical figure is Mundari araṛ ipilko (Hoffmann).

entries.sky_object: Three small stars near Orion's Belt (the belt itself, or the sword)
entries.region: Santal Parganas, Jharkhand / adjoining Bengal and Odisha
entries.literal_meaning: the yoke that shows itself off
entries.usage_note: Named only inside Bodding's entry for the Pleiades, as the thing to which the Pleiades-mallet belongs.
entries.citation: Bodding, A Santal Dictionary, vol. V (1936), s.v. sɘren (ipil), p. 352
entries.quote: the arar lalakko (three small stars near the belt of Orion)
entries.notes: Bodding glosses the group as 'three small stars NEAR the belt', which read strictly points at the sword of Orion; Campbell's arar is unambiguously the belt. Recorded separately rather than merged because the discrepancy is real. lalak is in Campbell 'to show off, as one showing what he can do in dancing'.

entries.sky_object: The head of Scorpius with Antares

modern_star.common_name: Antares and the three stars of the Scorpion's head
modern_star.bayer: α Sco with β, δ, σ Sco

entries.region: Santal Parganas, Jharkhand / adjoining Bengal and Odisha
entries.literal_meaning: a clod-crusher, a harrow without teeth
entries.usage_note: A farming implement seen in the sky: three stars in a line with a fourth at the apex.
entries.citation: Campbell, A Santali-English Dictionary (1899), s.v. Argom, p. 20
entries.quote: Argom. A constellation so named. It is part of the constellation Scorpio, and is composed of 4 stars, three of which are in line, and the other at the apex of the triangle. The star at the apex is Antares, or cor scorpii, a star of 1st. magnitude.
entries.notes: Deliberately not equated with Jyeṣṭhā: the nakshatra is Antares with σ and τ Sco, whereas Argom is a four-star harrow whose apex happens to be Antares. Campbell's separate homonym entry Argom 'a clod crusher, a harrow without teeth' fixes the literal sense.

entries.sky_object: Ursa Major — the bowl of the Big Dipper

modern_star.bayer: α, β, γ, δ Ursae Majoris

entries.region: Santal Parganas, Jharkhand / adjoining Bengal and Odisha
entries.citation: Campbell, A Santali-English Dictionary (1899), s.v. Buḍhi parkom ipil, p. 79
entries.quote: Buḍhi parkom ipil. The four chief stars in the body of the "Great Bear."
entries.notes: Campbell's neighbouring entries fix the elements: 'Budhi. An old woman'; parkom is the string cot. The same figure — an old woman's cot with the three handle stars as thieves — is recorded independently for Kurukh (khaṭī-pāwā bīnkō with ḍhālbar), for Gondi (Sedona Katul with Kalher) and for the Chhattisgarhi Dhuri (Russell 1916). Campbell does not name the three trailing stars.

entries.region: Santal Parganas, Jharkhand / adjoining Bengal and Odisha
entries.usage_note: The Milky Way as the road people walk to the weekly hāṭ.
entries.citation: Campbell, A Santali-English Dictionary (1899), s.v. Hat dahar / Panjar dahar, p. 223
entries.quote: Hat dahar. Panjar dahar. The Milky-way.
entries.notes: hāṭ is the periodic village market, dahar the road. A road-of-traffic image, like the Mundari 'cattle road' and the Gondi 'path of the animals', and quite unlike Sanskrit Ākāśagangā, a river.

entries.region: Santal Parganas, Jharkhand / adjoining Bengal and Odisha
entries.citation: Campbell, A Santali-English Dictionary (1899), s.v. Panjar dahar, p. 473 (also given s.v. Hat dahar, p. 223)
entries.quote: Panjar dahar. The Milky-way.
entries.notes: Given twice by Campbell, under Hat dahar and under Panjar 'a rib, the part of the body in which the ribs are'. The literal reading 'rib road' follows that headword, but Campbell does not gloss the compound.

entries.region: Santal Parganas, Jharkhand / adjoining Bengal and Odisha
entries.usage_note: Part of a Santal figure in Lyra: two small stars are a pigeon's eggs and the bright star beside them is the thief that comes for them.
entries.citation: Campbell, A Santali-English Dictionary (1899), s.v. Bele kombro, p. 51
entries.quote: Bele kombro. The egg stealer, a star so called, probably Vega.
entries.notes: Campbell himself hedges ('probably Vega'), so the identification is his and is graded likely. The compound is transparent from his own entries: 'Bele. An egg', and kombro 'thief'. The final syllable of kombro is illegible in both Internet Archive scans (printed 'kombroio' and 'kombroiii').

modern_star.common_name: Epsilon Lyrae, the double-double beside Vega

entries.region: Santal Parganas, Jharkhand / adjoining Bengal and Odisha
entries.citation: Campbell, A Santali-English Dictionary (1899), s.v. Potam bele, p. 512
entries.quote: Potam bele. Epsilon Lyrae, two small stars very close to each other, near Vega, in the constellation Lyra.
entries.notes: potam is the imperial pigeon, Carpophaga sylvatica (Campbell s.v.), bele an egg. The bird-and-eggs motif recurs across the whole set with different stars attached: Mundari puts the dove at Aldebaran with two egg stars beside it, Gondi puts Purad and Mes east of Sirius. Santali is the only one that also supplies the thief.

entries.region: Santal Parganas, Jharkhand / adjoining Bengal and Odisha
entries.citation: Campbell, A Santali-English Dictionary (1899), s.v. Candbol ipil, p. 89
entries.quote: Candbol ipil. A comet.
entries.notes: candbol is 'a tail' in Campbell (cf. 'Candbol tuthagetaea. His tail is short'). Hoffmann thought the matching Mundari caḍlom ipil 'tail star' was coined by missionaries; Campbell's independent Santali entry weakens that, though both men worked in mission circles.

entries.region: Santal Parganas, Jharkhand / adjoining Bengal and Odisha
entries.citation: Campbell, A Santali-English Dictionary (1899), s.v. Ic', p. 244
entries.quote: Ipil ic'kedae. The star voided excrement. (A shooting star is regarded as the excrement of another star.)
entries.notes: The identical explanation is recorded for Mundari (ipilko ic', Hoffmann) and for Gondi (sukum pelkta, Vahia & Halkare). It follows from the belief that the stars are living beings.

entries.sky_object: Aldebaran and the Hyades, surviving as a sowing season
entries.region: Santal Parganas, Jharkhand / adjoining Bengal and Odisha
entries.usage_note: Not used by Santals as a star at all but as the sowing week: the 13th of Jeṭ and the six days following. Paddy, maize, pumpkins and beans sown in Ruhni are said to come up strong. A cow-dung streak is drawn round the house wall on the first day to keep snakes off, and the ojha begins teaching his disciples.
entries.citation: Bodding, A Santal Dictionary, vol. V (1936), s.v. ruhni, p. 133
entries.quote: ruhni, n. The 13th day of the month of jeṭ and the following six days, in all seven days ... The ruhni is considered the proper and lucky time for sowing paddy, also Indian corn and pumpkins, beans, etc.
entries.notes: Flagged sanskritic because the word is Rohiṇī and Bodding says so, adding the Puranic genealogy from his own reading. What is interesting is the direction of the borrowing: the nakshatra has entered Santali as an agricultural week, not as a star. No Santal informant in Bodding identifies ruhni with Aldebaran.

entries.region: Santal Parganas, Jharkhand / adjoining Bengal and Odisha
entries.citation: Bodding, A Santal Dictionary, vol. V (1936), s.v. sukąr, sukro, sukur ipil, c. pp. 370-372
entries.quote: sukro, n. The planet Venus as an evening star. (H. sukr; only in books.)
entries.notes: Bodding's parenthesis '(only in books)' is the point of the entry: the Sanskrit/Hindi planet name is attested in Santali print but not in Santal speech. He marks Sani 'the planet Saturn' the same way. This is the clearest statement in any of these dictionaries that the graha system did not take.

entries.region: Santal Parganas, Jharkhand / adjoining Bengal and Odisha
entries.citation: Bodding, A Santal Dictionary, vol. V (1936), s.v. sin ipil, p. 284
entries.quote: sin ipil, n. The day-star (v. sub ipil).
entries.notes: Bodding refers the reader to the article ipil in an earlier volume; only vol. V of the Santal Dictionary is on the Internet Archive, so the identification could not be checked. 'Day-star' would most naturally be the morning star, but the sun itself is sin cando in the neighbouring entry, so the sense is not settled here.

entries.region: Santal Parganas, Jharkhand / adjoining Bengal and Odisha
entries.citation: Campbell, A Santali-English Dictionary (1899), s.v. Kaemaiya, p. 289
entries.quote: Kaemaiya. A constellation so named.
entries.notes: Recorded deliberately. Campbell gives no identification and cross-refers only to kaumau 'to make a loud noise'. Nothing in Bodding vol. V or in Hoffmann answers to it. An honest gap rather than a guess.

entries.region: Santal Parganas, Jharkhand / adjoining Bengal and Odisha
entries.name_roman: Sin boṅga reak hopon ko (the sun-god's children)
entries.usage_note: Cosmological frame rather than a star name: the sun-god is male, his wife is the moon, and the stars are their children.
entries.citation: Bodding, A Santal Dictionary, vol. V (1936), s.v. Sin boṅga, p. 283
entries.quote: Sin boṅga, is male, his wife being Aindą condo, the moon, the stars being their children. (Muṇḍari sin boṅga.)
entries.notes: name_roman here is a descriptive phrase, not a lexical headword; the entry is included because this belief is what licenses the shooting-star-as-excrement idiom in both Santali and Mundari. Bodding adds that the old gurus say the Santals have confused Sin boṅga with God, 'whose name they have forgotten'.

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: Part of a ploughing tableau: the middle star is the plough itself and the two outer ones the team of bullocks. Hoffmann's informants also used the group to tell the hour — 'ararako hasurtana, Orion is on the western horizon'.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925
entries.quote: (1) araṛd ipilko, the yoke stars, the three stars in Orion's belt. The middle one is supposed to represent the plough; and the two others, the team of bullocks
entries.notes: Printed 'arard-' in the scan; Hoffmann's retroflex ṛ with a subscript dot is regularly OCR'd as 'rd'. Cognate with Santali arar (Campbell). Cross-referenced at vol. XIII col. 4011 s.v. sitan-ipil and at vol. VI s.v. hasur and hāre.

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: Rigel is the ploughman himself, standing a little behind his team; Hoffmann notes the four stars form an elongated isosceles triangle with Rigel at the apex, which is what suggested the ploughman's stance.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925
entries.quote: sitan-ipil sbst., the ploughing star, i.e., Rigel. Sitan ipilko, the ploughing stars, i.e., the group formed by the ploughman Rigel and his team, the three stars in Orion's belt (araṛd ipilko).
entries.notes: Quoted from the separate headword at Encyclopaedia Mundarica vol. XIII col. 4011 (https://archive.org/download/dli.ernet.14932/), which confirms the reading given in the ipil article.

entries.sky_object: Rigel with Orion's Belt (the ploughing group)

modern_star.common_name: Rigel with the three belt stars

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: The arrival of this group in the evening sky is the sign for the farming season.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925
entries.quote: (3) sitan ipilko, the ploughing stars, the group formed by these four stars.

modern_star.common_name: two of the fainter stars in Orion's sword

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: Mice turned up by the ploughshare in the tableau; roasted mice are a much-coveted delicacy.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. III, s.v. cuṭu ipilkiŋ, col. 936; also vol. VII s.v. ipil col. 1920
entries.quote: cuṭu ipilkiŋ, sbst., the two mice stars, the two smaller stars visible in Orion's dagger.
entries.notes: The dual suffix -kiŋ is grammatical: exactly two stars. Hoffmann calls them fifth-magnitude stars 'in Orion's dagger'; he gives no Bayer letters and none are supplied here.

entries.sky_object: A star at the point of Orion's Sword

modern_star.common_name: the brighter star at the point of Orion's sword

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.literal_meaning: the one who has spitted the mice
entries.usage_note: The ploughman's small son, who has skewered the two mice on a splinter of bamboo to roast them; the three stars lie on a straight line.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. III, s.v. cuṭu gutu'keḍ ipil, col. 936
entries.quote: cuṭu gutu'keḍ ipil sbst., the star which holds the pinned mice, the harder and more southern of the three stars in Orion's dagger.
entries.notes: 'harder' in the scan is an OCR corruption, most probably for 'harder to see' or 'larger'.

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: The mallet the ploughman flung at a dove on her nest, aimed too high; it fell where the Pleiades are. In a second version heard south of Ranchi it is Siṅgboṅga who was chiselling a yoke and a plough to teach men to plough, and who threw the mallet at the dove.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925
entries.quote: (6) moṅgaru ipilko, the wooden mallet flung by the ploughman, the Pleiads. These are a cluster of seven stars of which six are visible to the naked eye; but the Mundas have sharp eyes ... The man who pointed them out to us, saw seven of them
entries.notes: Confirms Bodding's Santali gloss that the Pleiades are 'the mallet of the arar lalakko'. Hoffmann adds Ovid's quae septem dici, sex tamen esse solent, and notes his informant counted seven.

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. III, s.v. cuṭu rapa ipilko, col. 937
entries.quote: cuṭu rapa ipilko sbst., ltly., the mouse roasting stars, i.e. the Pleiades.
entries.notes: A second Mundari name for the cluster, attaching it to the mice of the Orion tableau rather than to the mallet. Hoffmann does not mention it in the long ipil article; it comes from the alphabetical entry.

entries.sky_object: Faint stars inside the Great Square of Pegasus

modern_star.common_name: Upsilon and Tau Pegasi and neighbours

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: The dying embers of the fire the threshing-floor watchman keeps under his cot on cold nights. Hoffmann adds that Mundas who do not know the maraṅ parkom group transfer the name to the Pleiades.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925
entries.quote: Near the middle of the Great Square there are a few small stars, amongst which Upsilon and Tau, just numerous enough to suggest a fire of dying embers. So these are the bursi ipilko.
entries.notes: Also entered separately at vol. II s.v. Bursi-ipilko, 'a group of stars described under ipil'. The transferred use for the Pleiades is recorded by Hoffmann as a mistake of his informants, which is itself worth keeping.

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: Three men creep up on a sleeping watchman to steal embers from the fire under his cot; two of them are these stars, lying west of the bed on a line pointing at the fire.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925
entries.quote: The fire thieves, bursi repą ipilkiŋ, are Lambda and Iota to the West of the bed, on a line pointing to the fire.
entries.notes: Two names for the same pair: Encyclopaedia Mundarica vol. II gives the headword Bursi-kumbuṛu-ipilko (kumbuṛu 'thief'), the ipil article gives bursi repą ipilkiŋ (repą 'to steal from one another').

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: The third fire-thief, who cannot help laughing at the discomfiture awaiting the sleeper, and whom the others push aside for fear he will wake the man.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925
entries.quote: The one who cannot help laughing, the laṇḍae ipil, is Delta of Cygnus.
entries.notes: Hoffmann's own identification, and geometrically awkward: δ Cygni lies a long way from Pegasus. He says himself, of the whole attempt to place these figures near the Pleiades, that it 'is rather a failure'. Recorded with the printed identification and the doubt attached.

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: The dove flushed off her nest by the ploughman's mallet, which alighted a little way off to wait until the enemy had gone.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925
entries.quote: (7) putam ipil, the dove started from her nest, Aldebaran, one of the Hyades, the star counted ninth in brightness.
entries.notes: Santali potam is the imperial pigeon (Campbell). Hoffmann uses this entry to correct M.B. Bhaduri's paper in Man in India, which had taken his informant's rohṛa — the name of a beetle that appears for two or three days at the end of May — for Hindi Rohiṇī, i.e. Aldebaran.

entries.sky_object: Two faint stars north of Aldebaran

modern_star.common_name: two fourth-magnitude stars north of Aldebaran

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: The two eggs left in the dove's nest. Hoffmann remarks that there are never more than two eggs in a dove's nest, which is why the dual is right.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925
entries.quote: (8) jarom ipilkiŋ, the two eggs in the dove's nest, two small stars of the fourth magnitude close together, North of Aldebaran, E. S. E. of the Pleiads.
entries.notes: No Bayer letters given by Hoffmann; none supplied here.

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: In the version heard in villages south of Ranchi, where the belt is the yoke Siṅgboṅga was chiselling, the plough itself is Rigel.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925
entries.quote: the yoke is represented by the three Kings (the three stars in Orion's belt), and the plough, nahel ipil, by Rigel.
entries.notes: Printed 'naVal ipil' in the better of the two scans; nahel is the ordinary Mundari and Santali word for a plough and the gloss 'the plough' is Hoffmann's own, so the reading is secure enough to record.

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.literal_meaning: the star under which the game grazes
entries.usage_note: Deer are believed to graze only while this star is above the horizon — a hunter's star, from the days when the forests were denser and game was an important part of the daily food.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. jilu-atiŋ ipil, col. 2065; the story at cols. 1920-1921
entries.quote: jilu-atiŋ-ipil sbst., Canopus. Game is believed to graze only whilst this star is above the horizon.
entries.notes: jilu now means game in general in Mundari; Hoffmann notes its Santali cognate jel is still restricted to deer. Sanskrit Agastya is the same star but an entirely unrelated figure, the sage.

entries.sky_object: The Great Square of Pegasus with Alpheratz

modern_star.bayer: α Andromedae; β, α, γ Pegasi

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.name_roman: maraṅ parkom ipilko; Siṅgboṅga gitikente parkom ipilko
entries.literal_meaning: the great bed stars; the bed Siṅgboṅga sleeps on
entries.usage_note: On so great and splendid a bed none but Siṅgboṅga can be supposed to sleep.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925
entries.quote: A great bed is seen there, viz., the Great Square delineated by Alpharatz in Andromeda, and Scheat, Markab, Algenib in Pegasus. These four stars are the maraṅ parkom ipilko, also called Siṅgboṅga gitikenteą parkom ipilko
entries.notes: parkom is the same string cot that Santali makes into the old woman's bed in Ursa Major. The Mundas run the cot image through four parts of the sky: the god's bed here, the co-wives' bed in Lupus, the bier in Ursa Major, and the watchman's pallet implied by the ember stars.

modern_star.common_name: Alpha, Beta, Mu and Rho Lupi

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: The bed two co-wives are fighting over — that is, the mastership of the house.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VI, s.v. hirumea parkom ipilko, cols. 1751-1757
entries.quote: The bed, hirumea parkom ipilko, is situated in Lupus, to the N. E. of the Southern Cross, and is represented by four stars, Alpha, Beta, Mu and Ro, which delineate a nearly equilateral parallelogram.
entries.notes: hirumea is the Mundari term for the relationship between two co-wives (vol. VI s.v.).

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.name_roman: hirumea repą ipilkiŋ; parkom repą ipilkiŋ
entries.literal_meaning: the two stars trying to steal the co-wife status — or the bed — from one another
entries.usage_note: The two co-wives pulling at opposite corners of the bed, which is why the parallelogram is out of square. Delta Centauri is the brighter and lies a little closer to the bed because, the Mundas say, she is the first wife and has gained the upper hand.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VI, s.v. hirumea repą ipilkiŋ, cols. 1751-1757
entries.quote: hirumea repą ipilkiŋ sbst, ltly., the two stars trying to steal from each other the relationship of co-wives, i.e., trying to oust each other from the status of first wife. They are also called parkom repą ipilkiŋ, the two stars trying to steal a bed from each other.
entries.notes: One of the very few star names anywhere that encodes a point of domestic law rather than a season or a trade.

entries.sky_object: Ursa Major — the bowl of the Big Dipper, with Alioth and Mizar

modern_star.common_name: Dubhe, Merak, Phecda, Megrez, with Alioth and Mizar
modern_star.bayer: α, β, γ, δ (+ ε, ζ) Ursae Majoris

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: The cot doubles as the bier that carries a corpse to the grave; after the burial one side of the frame is broken and the bed left at the burial ground. The watchman on the threshing floor, waking cold before dawn, sees the broken frame in the north, and in Alioth and Mizar the mourners walking away from the grave.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925
entries.quote: The quadrangle with these sad associations is called topagara parkom ipilko, the bier stars.
entries.notes: The first element is printed topagara/topogara in the two scans and could not be checked against its own alphabetical entry, since Encyclopaedia Mundarica vols. IX, XI and XIV-XVI are not on the Internet Archive; the reading of the first word is therefore unresolved and only 'the bier stars' is secure. Note how far this is from Saptarṣi — the same four stars, an entirely different mood.

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: The village blacksmith, sitting and watching his smithy fire.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925
entries.quote: Capella, the fourth star in order of magnitude, is the blacksmith and therefore called barai ipil.
entries.notes: Reading of the first element unresolved — the two scans print 'baraiipil' and 'hnrai^ipV', and the alphabetical entry would fall in a volume not available. The gloss 'the blacksmith' is unambiguous.

entries.sky_object: Two stars at the base of a triangle in Auriga
entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: The blacksmith's double bellows; Epsilon Aurigae is the sharp vertex of the isosceles triangle whose base they form, and is the smithy fire.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925
entries.quote: He sits watching the smithy fire ... This star, Epsilon, is the sharp vertex of an isosceles triangle, the base of which is formed by his double bellows, capua ipilkiŋ.
entries.notes: Compare Kurukh, where the blacksmith's bellows (lohrā-capuā bīnkō) is the name of the Pleiades and not of a figure in Auriga. Same implement, same word, different stars — good evidence that the naming is independent rather than borrowed one way.

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.name_roman: gaiko hora, gaiko hor, gaikoiḍ, caṭar
entries.usage_note: The village cattle-road along which the herd is driven out a little before dawn and led back at night. Siṅgboṅga's cattle are driven along it by Lugu, his cowherd.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. V, s.v. gaiko hor / gaiko hora, col. 1356; the account at vol. VII s.v. ipil, col. 1923
entries.quote: gaiko hor, gaiko hora sbst., the milky way : gaiko horare kub hupuri hupuri ipilko menakoa, in the milky way there are a great number of small stars.
entries.notes: caṭar is the Sadani word for the village main road, haṭia the Mundari. Kurukh has the same image (gāy-chour bīnkō, the cattle-track) and Gondi likewise (Dhor Sari, the path of the animals) — a shared central-Indian reading of the galaxy that owes nothing to Ākāśagangā.

modern_star.common_name: Venus, or any planet rising before the sun

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.name_roman: Lugu ipil, mahara ipil, gaikohaṛ ipil
entries.usage_note: Lugu is the cowherd in Siṅgboṅga's service, and is visible only when, like the maharas on earth, he drives the cattle out a little before dawn.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925
entries.quote: Lugu ipil or mahara ipil is no other than the Morning star.
entries.notes: Cross-entered at vol. V col. 1357: 'gaikohaṛ-ipil syn. of mahara ipil'. Hoffmann observes that the Mundas make no distinction between stars and planets and never noticed that planets do not twinkle.

modern_star.common_name: Venus or any planet rising before the sun

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: The star that heralds dawn; aṅgo-dipli is 'at dawn, at daybreak'.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. I, s.v. aṅgo-ipil
entries.quote: aṅgo-ipil syn. of burkaipil, sbst., the morning star, i. e., Mars, Saturn, Jupiter and Venus when they happen to rise a little before dawn.
entries.notes: Hoffmann's ipil article gives two further names for the morning star: burka ipil, which he says is a corruption of Hindi bhor kā tārā and so a Sadan loan, and a compound meaning 'the star which drives home the thieves, warning them that the light of day is coming', whose Mundari form is too badly OCR'd in both scans to record — its first element is evidently kumbuṛu, 'thief'.

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: Comets portend public calamities. The name is from joṅg, the broom the Mundas sweep their houses with.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925
entries.quote: They see a striking resemblance between them and the brooms, joṅg, with which they sweep their houses. A comet is therefore called joṅg ipil.
entries.notes: Hoffmann adds that caḍlom ipil, 'tail star', is also heard but 'seems to have been first coined by Missionaries'. Campbell's independent Santali Candbol ipil suggests otherwise. The broom image is shared with Kurukh (calkī bīnkō) and Gondi (kayshar, jhāḍani, bahārī).

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: Most noticeable about the middle of November, when the threshing floors are made and must be watched at night. 'Tonight the stars have many evacuations.'
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925
entries.quote: They call them ipilko ic', the excrements of the stars! ... Remember that the stars are living beings, the children of the moon.

entries.sky_object: Venus and a bright star or planet beside it
entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand
entries.name_roman: Sukura and Sukurani; lagan ipilkiŋ, logon ipilkiŋ
entries.literal_meaning: Sukra and Sukrani; the two stars that fix the marriage date
entries.usage_note: In the Hasada country and the Karra police subdivision their close conjunction is read by animists as a very favourable omen for marriages contracted in that month or year — the stars are said to be loving and kissing each other. Elsewhere in Nagpur they are unknown, as is the logon-tol ceremony itself.
entries.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925
entries.quote: two stars, Sukura and Sukurani, also called lagan ipilkiŋ, logon ipilkiŋ, which are an evident loan from the Sadans or the Hinduized aborigines, and present the only little touch of astrology discoverable in the star lore of the Mundas
entries.notes: Flagged sanskritic on Hoffmann's own analysis. He notes that Sukrani exists in no Hindu system: for the Mundas she is whatever bright star or planet happens to sit near Venus in a given year. This is the only astrology Hoffmann found in the whole of Munda sky-lore, and he is emphatic that the Munda 'neither knows, nor cares to know, what a horoscope is'.

modern_star.common_name: Venus (or any planet rising before the sun)

entries.region: Kolhan, Singhbhum, Jharkhand
entries.citation: Burrows, Ho Grammar, with Vocabulary (1915), English-Ho vocabulary s.v. 'morning star', and Ho-English vocabulary s.v. anyo ipil
entries.quote: anyo ipil (n. a.) morning star
entries.notes: Directly cognate with Mundari aṅgo ipil. Burrows' scan carries no usable page numbers in its OCR, so the citation is by headword only. Ho is the one Munda language of the three for which no dictionary on Hoffmann's or Bodding's scale exists, and Burrows records no constellation names at all.

entries.region: Kolhan, Singhbhum, Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: Burrows uses the word as his paradigm for the animate noun class, alongside 'man'.
entries.citation: Burrows, Ho Grammar, with Vocabulary (1915), on the animate and inanimate noun classes
entries.quote: ipil - a star, ipilking - two stars, ipilko - three or more stars ; but daru - one or more trees
entries.notes: Included because it is grammatical evidence for the belief the ethnographers record separately: in Ho, as in Mundari and Santali, stars belong to the animate class along with people and animals, while trees do not. The dual in the Mundari star names (cuṭu ipilkiŋ, jarom ipilkiŋ) is the same category at work.

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau (Oraon country), Jharkhand
entries.citation: Grignard, An Oraon-English Dictionary (1924), s.v. ugtā, p. 684; also s.v. bīnkō, p. 85
entries.quote: Ugtā-pagṛī, the plough. — Ugtā-pagṛī bīnkō, constellation of Orion.
entries.notes: Grignard's long entry s.v. ugtā describes the parts of the Oraon plough in detail, so the metaphor is documented from the implement upwards. The same reading of Orion as Gondi Nangar/Nangal and, at one remove, the Mundari ploughing tableau.

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau (Oraon country), Jharkhand
entries.name_roman: lohrā-capuā bīnkō; capuā bīnkō; pārkī bīnkō
entries.citation: Grignard, An Oraon-English Dictionary (1924), s.v. bīnkō, p. 85; s.v. capuā, p. 128; s.v. lohrā, p. 465
entries.quote: Lohrā-capuā bīnkō, name of a constellation also called pārkī bīnkō.
entries.notes: Three entries agree that the bellows constellation is the Pleiades (s.v. capuā: 'Capuā-binko, the constellation of the Pleiades'). pārkī, given as a synonym, is elsewhere in Grignard a kind of dove — whether the same word is meant is not stated and is not assumed here.

entries.sky_object: Ursa Major — the bowl of the Big Dipper, and the three handle stars

modern_star.common_name: Dubhe, Merak, Phecda, Megrez, with Alioth, Mizar and Alkaid
modern_star.bayer: α, β, γ, δ (+ ε, ζ, η) Ursae Majoris

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau (Oraon country), Jharkhand
entries.name_roman: khaṭī-pāwā bīnkō (the three outside stars: ḍhālbar)
entries.usage_note: The quadrangle is the bed; the three stars outside it are ḍhālbar, thieves, after the bedstead.
entries.citation: Grignard, An Oraon-English Dictionary (1924), s.v. khaṭī, p. 415 (thief: s.v. ḍhālbās, p. 403)
entries.quote: Khaṭī-pāwā binko, lit. the cot-feet constellation, i. e. the Great Bear (or rather, the quadrangle in the Great Bear — the three outside stars being called ḍhālbar, or thieves) of the aforesaid bedstead.
entries.notes: The single most widely shared indigenous figure in this compilation: cot plus three thieves, attested independently in Kurukh (Dravidian), Santali (Munda), Gondi (Dravidian) and among the Chhattisgarhi Dhuri. Grignard prints the plural ḍhālbar; his headword is ḍhālbās, 'a thief'.

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau (Oraon country), Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: chour is the broad way for the cattle, from the skirts of the village up to the main road.
entries.citation: Grignard, An Oraon-English Dictionary (1924), s.v. gāy, p. 256; s.v. chour, p. 166
entries.quote: chour S. The broad way for the cattle, from the skirts of the village up to the main road. Gāy-chour, the milky way.

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau (Oraon country), Jharkhand
entries.literal_meaning: the dawn star; the dusk star
entries.citation: Grignard, An Oraon-English Dictionary (1924), s.v. bijj-bīnkō, p. 82; s.v. bhurkā, p. 114; s.v. bīnkō, p. 85
entries.quote: bhurkā s. The star Venus. Bhurkā-bīnkō. — Syn. Bijj-bīnkō (morning star), ḍhurti-bīnkō (evening star.)
entries.notes: bijj- is the same element as bijj-ghaṛī 'dawn, peep of day' and bijjnā 'to dawn'. bhurkā is cognate with the Mundari Sadan loan burka ipil (< Hindi bhor kā tārā).

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau (Oraon country), Jharkhand
entries.usage_note: The appearance of a comet is read as an omen: 'a comet has appeared; we may have this year a famine as well as a plenteous crop.'
entries.citation: Grignard, An Oraon-English Dictionary (1924), s.v. calkī, p. 123; s.v. bīnkō, p. 85
entries.quote: Calkī S. 1. A special kind of grass, from which the Indian broom is made ... Calkī-bīnkō, comet.

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau (Oraon country), Jharkhand
entries.citation: Grignard, An Oraon-English Dictionary (1924), s.v. chir'u, p. 164; s.v. bīnkō, p. 85
entries.quote: Chir'u. Chir'u binko, shooting star
entries.notes: Kurukh does not share the Munda 'star excrement' idiom for meteors; Grignard's other phrase is simply 'there, a star is shooting'.

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau (Oraon country), Jharkhand
entries.citation: Grignard, An Oraon-English Dictionary (1924), s.v. mugrā, sense 2
entries.notes: Grignard's second sense of mugrā 'a mallet' is 'Name of a constellation', followed by a Kurukh name that the Internet Archive scan renders unreadably (printed 'Ahi^ta-binko'); the page number is likewise lost in that stretch of bad OCR, so no quote is given. Flagged rather than dropped, because Mundari names the Pleiades muṅgaru ipilko, 'the mallet stars', and Santali says the Pleiades are the mallet of the yoke — a Kurukh mallet constellation is very likely the same figure, but this could not be verified.

entries.region: Chota Nagpur plateau (Oraon country), Jharkhand
entries.citation: Grignard, An Oraon-English Dictionary (1924), s.v. bīnkō, p. 85
entries.quote: bīnkō S. star.

entries.region: Nilgiri hills, Tamil Nadu
entries.usage_note: Held to be six stars, not seven: Kadsht had six men and Keirt only one, and Keirt broke the leg of one of the six, so that five now stand close together and one lags behind. Because of that quarrel the god ruled that Kadsht and Keirt must never be in the sky together. At one funeral the setting of Kadsht and the appearance of Keirt was the sign that the azaramkedr might begin.
entries.citation: Rivers, The Todas (1906), ch. XXIV 'Constellations and Stars', pp. 593-594
entries.quote: The Pleiades are called Kadsht and the constellation is believed to be composed of six stars.
entries.notes: One of very few traditions anywhere that counts the cluster as six rather than seven and has a story for the missing one.

modern_star.common_name: the stars in the sword of Orion

entries.region: Nilgiri hills, Tamil Nadu
entries.usage_note: The sword stars are a porcupine, and the three stars of the belt are trying to escape from it.
entries.citation: Rivers, The Todas (1906), p. 594
entries.quote: A group of stars called Pŏdimīn, or porcupine star, corresponds to the stars in the sword of Orion. They are regarded as a porcupine from which the three stars of the belt are trying to escape.
entries.notes: Two Internet Archive scans print the name as 'Pbdimin' and 'PbdimiUy'; the reading Pŏdimīn is supported by Katikālmin, where -mīn is evidently 'star', and by Rivers' own glossary, which gives podi for the porcupine (p. 267) and mul for its quills. Note that this reverses the Munda and Gondi reading of the same region of sky: for them the belt is a plough or a yoke and the sword is mice or a hunter's kill.

entries.region: Nilgiri hills, Tamil Nadu
entries.citation: Rivers, The Todas (1906), p. 594
entries.quote: A constellation of seven stars is called Katikālmin. From the description it appeared to be the Great Bear. This constellation was not visible, but when I made a drawing of its seven chief stars, it was at once recognised as Katikālmin.
entries.notes: Rivers' method — he drew the seven stars and had the drawing named — is unusually good practice for 1906 and is why this is graded likely rather than disputed. He gives no meaning for the name. Alone among the traditions here, the Toda Ursa Major is not a cot.

entries.region: Nilgiri hills, Tamil Nadu
entries.usage_note: Corresponds to the Badaga etukadichi, 'bull deceiving': a Badaga once saw a star so bright he took it for the morning star and let his bulls out of the pen; when day did not come he said, let the star be called etukadichi.
entries.citation: Rivers, The Todas (1906), pp. 594-595
entries.quote: A single star called Ishtkati is almost certainly Sirius.
entries.notes: Rivers is careful: Jupiter was pointed out to him as Ishtkati at first and he rejects that. The story attached is a Badaga one and Rivers treats the name as borrowed.

modern_star.common_name: two stars near Aldebaran, in the Hyades

entries.region: Nilgiri hills, Tamil Nadu
entries.literal_meaning: the young of the tūdrval bird
entries.usage_note: A bird with young was left by its mother while she went for food; a snake climbed the tree, and the nestlings called to Kudursami, who took them up into the sky. The tūdrval still sings 'Kudursami trrrrrrr'. In another version the bird had offended Swami, who took its young as a punishment.
entries.citation: Rivers, The Todas (1906), p. 595
entries.quote: The name of the bird was tūdrval, and so one star is called tudrvalmokh.
entries.notes: Rivers names a pair; the second name is printed 'Tidiishti' in both Internet Archive scans and could not be resolved, so it is not given here. The Bayer letters are Rivers' own conjecture ('probably γ and ε Tauri'). He considers the story a recent acquisition from Indian folk-tale — worth weighing against the fact that the same bird-and-nestlings figure turns up in Santali, Mundari and Gondi at other stars.

entries.region: Nilgiri hills, Tamil Nadu
entries.citation: Rivers, The Todas (1906), p. 593
entries.quote: The Todas know Venus, which they call Pili, and they also speak of the "morning star."

entries.region: Nilgiri hills, Tamil Nadu
entries.usage_note: Feared above all after childbirth; its evil influence is keirtpudrtviti, and the whole seclusion-hut procedure is designed to avert it. Said to be always near the sun, and never in the same part of the sky as the Pleiades.
entries.citation: Rivers, The Todas (1906), pp. 593-594 (and ch. XIV, pp. 269, 326)
entries.quote: I think it most probable that this mysterious inhabitant of the sky is not a star at all, but a being allied to the Hindu Ketu.
entries.notes: Recorded precisely because it resists identification. Rivers could get no one to point it out and no account of where in the sky it stands, and concludes it is probably Ketu under a Badaga name — yet at one funeral its 'appearance' was used as a timing signal, which he admits looks like a real body. Left unidentified.

entries.region: Khasi and Jaintia hills, Meghalaya
entries.citation: Nissor Singh, Khasi-English Dictionary (1906), s.v. Khlur, p. 33; s.v. 'lur, p. 120
entries.quote: Khlur, u, n. a star.

entries.region: Khasi and Jaintia hills, Meghalaya
entries.literal_meaning: the light star, the bright star
entries.citation: Nissor Singh, Khasi-English Dictionary (1906), s.v. 'lur-shai, p. 120
entries.quote: 'lur-shai, u, n. the morning star.
entries.notes: shai is 'light, bright' in the same dictionary.

entries.region: Khasi and Jaintia hills, Meghalaya
entries.citation: Nissor Singh, Khasi-English Dictionary (1906), s.v. 'lur-miet, p. 120
entries.quote: 'lur-miet, u, n. the evening star.
entries.notes: miet is 'night'.

entries.region: Khasi and Jaintia hills, Meghalaya
entries.citation: Nissor Singh, Khasi-English Dictionary (1906), s.v. 'lur-mangkara, p. 120; s.v. Mangkara, p. 127
entries.quote: 'lur-mangkara, u, n. the brightest star.
entries.notes: Entered twice by Nissor Singh but never identified with a particular star. Whether mangkara is connected with Sanskrit makara is not stated in the dictionary and is not assumed here.

entries.region: Khasi and Jaintia hills, Meghalaya
entries.citation: Nissor Singh, Khasi-English Dictionary (1906), s.v. 'lur-dih-duma, p. 120
entries.quote: 'lur-dih-duma, u, n. the comet.
entries.notes: dih is 'to drink', used of smoking, and duma 'tobacco', both in the same dictionary — the comet is the star with a pipe. The only figurative star name Khasi yielded, and quite unlike the broom that the Munda, Kurukh and Gondi languages all use.

entries.region: South Andaman (Aka-Bea and neighbouring tribes)
entries.usage_note: The only star or constellation in the Andamans that Man found to bear a name at all.
entries.citation: Man, On the Aboriginal Inhabitants of the Andaman Islands (1883), § 8, p. 118
entries.quote: Of all the stars and constellations Orion's belt alone is found to bear a name (bela-), but this is not to be wondered at, as they never venture upon any distant voyages, and do not therefore experience any necessity for studying the bearing of the various planets and constellations at different seasons
entries.notes: Man's trailing hyphen is his convention for a stem requiring a prefix. His explanation — no long voyages, therefore no need of star bearings — is his own inference and should be read as such; it is at least consistent with Radcliffe-Brown's independent finding forty years later in the North Andaman.

entries.region: South Andaman (Aka-Bea and neighbouring tribes)
entries.usage_note: Poetically described as the road used by the mòrowin-, the spirits Man renders 'angels'.
entries.citation: Man, On the Aboriginal Inhabitants of the Andaman Islands (1883), § 8, p. 118
entries.quote: Their astronomical observations have, however, extended to the discovery of the milky way, which they call ig-yádowa-, and poetically describe as the road used by the angels (mòrowin-).
entries.notes: The two Internet Archive scans of Man's paper print the name as 'ig-ydiowa-' and 'ig-gdlovrt-'; ig-yádowa- is the best reconstruction from them and the reading is unresolved pending a clean copy. The gloss 'road of the spirits' is secure and matches the road-reading of the galaxy found right across the Munda, Kurukh and Gond areas.

entries.sky_object: The stars, in two named classes
entries.region: North Andaman (Aka-Cari, Aka-Jeru)
entries.literal_meaning: a finely marked beetle; the common fire-fly
entries.usage_note: The sun is the wife of the moon and the stars are their children; the big children are named for a beetle and the little ones for the firefly.
entries.citation: Radcliffe-Brown, The Andaman Islanders (1922), ch. IV, p. 141
entries.quote: their children the stars are Catlo, the larger ones, and Katan the smaller. Catlo is the name of a species of finely marked beetle, and katan is the name of the common fire-fly. Individual stars or constellations are not recognized.
entries.notes: A first-class negative: the North Andamanese sort the stars by brightness into two named kinds of luminous insect and name no individual star at all. Radcliffe-Brown warns at the head of the same chapter that flatly contradictory statements are given by the same informant and both believed — a caution on the chapter as a whole, not on this sentence.

entries.region: Central Nicobars (Nancowry group)
entries.citation: Man, A Dictionary of the Central Nicobarese Language (1889), Nicobarese-English p. 207 s.v. tā-yan; English-Nicobarese p. 71 s.v. Pleiades
entries.quote: tā-yan, Pleiades.
entries.notes: Entered in both halves of the dictionary. Man gives no story and no calendrical use, and no other constellation name appears anywhere in the volume.

entries.sky_object: Ursa Major — the Big Dipper as a bier
entries.region: the Baiga chak and the surrounding country — Mandla, Baihar, Kawardha, Dindori and Rewa, in what was then the Central Provinces
entries.usage_note: A bed on which a corpse is carried out. When they bring it out it is night; when they put it back it is day. The Baiga smash the bed with their axes when they carry a corpse, which is why bits of the bed are scattered all over the sky.
entries.citation: Verrier Elwin, The Baiga (London: John Murray, 1939), p. 334
entries.quote: "It is a bed on which a corpse is carried out. When they bring it out, it is night ; when they put it back, it is day. When we carry a corpse, we always smash the bed with our axes. That is why bits of the bed are scattered all over the sky."
entries.notes: THE DEATH-COT, AND THE BEST-EXPLAINED VERSION OF IT IN THE DATABASE. Lambadi, Mundari and Teressa all make Ursa Major a bier rather than a bed; the Mundari name topoḍ-akan parkom ipilko even means the broken bed. Only the Baiga account says why the bed is broken, and then uses the breakage to explain the rest of the sky: the scattered stars are the splinters. The same account makes the daily rising and setting of the constellation the carrying out and bringing back of the corpse. Elwin gives it in his informants' words and this database quotes them. Elwin died in February 1964, so the Indian term of sixty years from the following year expired on 1 January 2025 and The Baiga is quoted verbatim here. The expansion plan listed Elwin among the sources to be paraphrased; that was written on the assumption he was still in copyright, and it is corrected rather than followed.

entries.sky_object: Ursa Major — the king's bed with the broken leg
entries.region: the Baiga chak and the surrounding country — Mandla, Baihar, Kawardha, Dindori and Rewa, in what was then the Central Provinces
entries.usage_note: In Baihar: a King and Queen quarrelled and the Queen ran to kill herself in the star called the Tank; the Kotwar ran to stop her; the King jumped out of bed so violently that one leg of the bed broke — which is why you always see one leg in the wrong place. In Mandla the same story is told with a Bhoi and Bhoin, a Gond man and woman, as hero and heroine.
entries.citation: Verrier Elwin, The Baiga (London: John Murray, 1939), p. 334
entries.quote: "The King was sitting on his bed and when he saw the Queen running towards the Tank, he jumped out of bed so violently that one leg of the bed broke — that is why you always see one leg in the wrong place."
entries.notes: A STORY BUILT TO EXPLAIN AN OBSERVED IRREGULARITY: the Big Dipper is not a true rectangle, and this is an account of the star that is out of line. Elwin adds the class point — the aristocratic Binjhwar Baiga make the hero a King, the Mandla Baiga make him a Gond villager, and it is the same story. Elwin died in February 1964, so the Indian term of sixty years from the following year expired on 1 January 2025 and The Baiga is quoted verbatim here. The expansion plan listed Elwin among the sources to be paraphrased; that was written on the assumption he was still in copyright, and it is corrected rather than followed.

caveats: Every name here was read from OCR of a scanned page, not from a keyed text. Colonial-era romanisations of Munda, Kurukh and Andamanese are dense with diacritics and the DjVu OCR loses them systematically: Hoffmann's retroflex ṛ comes out as 'rd', Bodding's hooked vowels as 'g' and 'q'. Where a form could be checked against a second scan of the same book, or against its own alphabetical entry elsewhere in the same work, that was done and the reading is given plainly. Where it could not, the notes say so and print what the scan actually shows. Four names are flagged in their notes as unresolved: Mundari topagara/topoḍ-akan, Mundari barai ipil, Santali bele kombro (final syllable) and Andamanese ig-yádowa-.

Nothing was quoted from a source in copyright. The twenty Gondi entries are paraphrased throughout from Vahia & Halkare (2013) and their quote fields are null; the same applies to the Bhil paper of 2023, which is cited in the summary as a lead and used for nothing else. Elwin's Baiga and Muria monographs were not used, for the same reason.

Modern identifications are the source's own except where the source gives none, in which case the fields are left empty and confidence is 'unidentified'. Nine entries carry that grade — Santali Kaemaiya and sin ipil, Kurukh mugrā, Khasi 'lur-mangkara, Toda Keirt, and Gondi Purad/Mes, Khala, Irukna Mara and Khayan — and they are kept rather than dropped, because an unidentified indigenous figure is a result. Seven more are graded 'disputed' where the sources disagree with each other or with themselves.

Page numbers were derived from the running heads of the specific Internet Archive scans cited, not from a physical copy, and for two-column dictionaries they may be out by one. Encyclopaedia Mundarica is cited by column number, which is how it is paginated. Burrows' Ho grammar has no recoverable page numbers in its OCR and is cited by headword only; Whitehead's Car-Nicobarese dictionary likewise.

Register is assigned as the source presents the material. 'sanskritic' marks the four cases where a community is recorded using a Sanskrit-derived term — Santali ruhni and sukro/Sani, Mundari Sukura/Sukurani, Gondi Dhruva Tara — and in every one of them the recording ethnographer says himself that the term is a loan, a book-word or a late addition. Those judgements are theirs, not mine.

Several of these sources are condescending about the people they describe, and that bears on reliability. Rivers concludes that most or all Toda star ideas are borrowed, a judgement he reaches partly on the assumption that Toda folklore is thin. Man explains the single Andamanese constellation name by saying the islanders 'never venture upon any distant voyages'. Hoffmann calls the Munda bed 'a miserable bed' and Munda star-folklore 'rather scanty' — immediately before filling seven columns with it. Russell's framing throughout is evolutionary. None of that editorialising is reproduced in the entries; where it affects what was collected, the notes say so.

The languages field carries one addition to the brief's list, Chhattisgarhi, for the three Dhuri entries from Russell & Hiralal. They are marked register 'folk', not 'tribal': the Dhuri are a caste, not an Adivasi community. They are here because they are the earliest printed witness to the cot-and-three-thieves figure that four tribal traditions independently share.

No Ho, Khasi, Andamanese or Nicobarese source consulted attached a story to a star name. For those communities this file records vocabulary, which is what survives; the narrative material is Munda, Santal, Kurukh, Gond and Toda.

Two leads were identified and not followed to the end: M.B. Bhaduri, 'Astronomy of the Mundas and their star names', Man in India, read at the second Oriental Conference and attacked at length by Hoffmann for its errors; and the JAHH series by Vahia, Halkare and colleagues on the Korku, Kolam, Banjara and Pardhi, which extends the same fieldwork to communities outside this file's language list.

THREE SOURCES ADDED ON A LATER PASS, all obtained from archive.org by way of the metadata endpoint after the ordinary download path had refused them. Their quotes are transcribed from the archive.org OCR, not from page images, because none of the three uses a diacritic the OCR could destroy; where the OCR has damaged an English word inside a quote the restoration is bracketed — 't[h]e', 'p[l].', '[li]ke' — and nothing is mended silently: Elwin's The Baiga (1939), Ramamurti's Sora-English Dictionary (1938) and Winfield's A Vocabulary of the Kui Language (1929). Elwin died in February 1964, so the Indian term expired on 1 January 2025 and he is quoted verbatim rather than paraphrased; the expansion plan had listed him among the in-copyright sources and that is corrected here.

The Baiga entries carry `language: Chhattisgarhi` with `community: Baiga`, not a language called Baigani. Elwin's own account is that the Baiga speak a form of the local Chhattisgarhi, and every name he records — Nangar, Kutela, Tengra, Chirai, Barhai, Dhimar, Jhal, Machhri, Dhanu, Ban, Sap, Chowkidar — is a transparent Chhattisgarhi or Hindi word. Filing them under an invented language would have made the database claim something Elwin does not. This is what the `community` field was added for.

THE BAIGA SKY IS FIFTEEN FIGURES AND ELWIN LOCATES ALMOST NONE OF THEM. He names the Great Bear, queries Orion once, and for the other thirteen gives the figure and no position at all. Eleven entries are therefore `unidentified`, which is the largest block of them in this database. That is the honest reading of an ethnographer who was recording what people said rather than surveying the sky, and the alternative — matching a carpenter, a fisherman and a hoe to constellations by guesswork — would be worthless.
